transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-04 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Eve (Redwood AE), Daniel (Redwood SE), Maya (Rivet - Head of ML), Liam (Rivet - Platform), Priya (Rivet - Security), Jon (Rivet intern)

Summary:
Quick demo/walkthrough of how to map existing OpenAI/Anthropic/Together endpoints to Redwood API, show console and Optimize suggestions, and align on pilot/benchmarks. Customer concerned about latency parity, streaming behavior, KMS and audit logs for Private deployment.

Topics covered:
- endpoint and param mapping (temperature, top_p, stop tokens)
- streaming and chunking differences
- KV cache and prefix caching for multi-turn
- batching and cost/latency tradeoffs
- dedicated vs hosted vs private (VPC/KMS)
- security artifacts (SOC2, SSO, audit logs)

Transcript body:
[00:00:03] Eve: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um — quick intros, I'm Eve, AE at Redwood, and with me is Daniel our solutions engineer.
[00:00:12] Daniel: hi hi, hello.
[00:00:15] Maya: Hi, Maya here. We run the recommendation models and chat helpers at Rivet, mainly on OpenAI and a bit of Anthropeek — sorry Anthropic, I always say it wrong.
[00:00:24] Eve: no worries — that's fine. Quick agenda: map endpoints, show the console, run a small live parity example, and then propose a benchmark plan.
[00:00:33] Liam: Sounds good — our big asks: match latency within ~20ms tail, preserve streaming tokens, and ensure we can keep data in our VPC for PCI concerns.
[00:00:42] Priya: And security: we need KMS + audit logs and SSO via SAML.
[00:00:46] Daniel: totally — we'll show the private options and what we usually do for KMS and audit retention.

[00:01:15] Daniel: Ok, starting with API parity — most of you are hitting something like openai.com/v1/chat/completions with model=..., messages array, temperature, top_p, n, stop, stream etc. Redwood exposes a single /v1/generate-like endpoint and supports both chat-structured and text prompts. So you can map messages -> input.messages, and the params map 1:1 for the most part.
[00:01:45] Maya: For Anthropic there are different max_tokens semantics and the stop token handling is weird — we saw truncation earlier. Any gotchas?
[00:01:53] Daniel: yeah Anthropic does that different chunking. In Redwood we normalize stop semantics and we also provide a compatibility flag for Anthro-style responses. There's a small difference in token counting for some tokenizers — recommend running that sample harness.
[00:02:12] Liam: What about Together models — they use a slightly different streaming protocol right?
[00:02:17] Daniel: Right — Together streams can be newline-chunked. Redwood supports chunked streaming and we have an SSE + websocket option. In practice clients just need to handle partial messages; our SDKs already do that.
[00:02:32] Jon: (soft) do we need to change our request shaping?
[00:02:35] Maya: We use a bunch of prompt engineering with system messages and a cached prefix; not sure how Redwood handles KV cache.
[00:02:42] Daniel: Redwood has prefix/KV cache at the runtime; if you pin a model variant we can cache common prefixes and reuse KV to reduce latency on multi-turn. That helps us avoid re-sending big system messages. Note: cache hits show up in the console metrics.
[00:03:01] Eve: demo time — console is up. (screen share noise) Here's the model catalog, we surface verified perf profiles, and here's the mapping helper — you paste your OpenAI/Anthropic/Together example and it emits the equivalent Redwood request.
[00:03:20] Maya: oh nice, does it also suggest quantization flags?
[00:03:23] Daniel: yes under Optimize we give recommendations — quantize to int8 or int4 depending on workload, but for parity mapping we typically keep the same fp16 for initial bench. We provide an estimated speedup and token cost delta.
[00:03:39] Liam: Can you show an example of a streaming chat?
[00:03:42] Daniel: (runs example) Sending prompt now... you'll see partial tokens appear, same as current client. Note: we intentionally keep chunk boundaries compatible with common clients.
[00:03:59] Maya: I noticed in earlier docs mention of fallback routing if a dedicated pool is saturated — can that flip without us having to change model names?
[00:04:07] Eve: Yes, we have smart routing — policy-based. You can set SLOs and fallback rules, if dedicated is saturated it can route to hosted or a lower-cost model variant automatically and we put a header in the response so you can detect fallback.
[00:04:22] Priya: That header, is it auditable in logs?
[00:04:25] Daniel: yes it surfaces in request-level logs and the audit trail.
[00:04:30] Priya: Good. What about data at rest — KMS support?
[00:04:34] Daniel: For Private deployments we integrate with customer KMS or HSM. For Hosted we offer customer-managed keys for sensitive workloads. We can share the KMS integration guide.
[00:04:44] Maya: Any SOC 2 artifacts?
[00:04:46] Eve: yes SOC 2 type II, plus ISO information in the security pack. We'll share exact certs.

[00:05:12] Daniel: Back to parity: the key is to map these specific items: tokenization differences, stop sequences, streaming chunk semantics, and system message handling. We recommend a three-stage approach: 1) equivalence mapping (one-off mapping sheet), 2) small functional pilot including time-limited traffic, 3) production benchmark run for latency/cost.
[00:05:35] Liam: For the benchmark, how do we measure tail latency and cost?
[00:05:38] Daniel: our benchmark harness collects p50/p90/p99 for token and request latency, and reports cost per generated token under different batching levels. We'll run your prompt set under the same concurrency as production.
[00:05:52] Maya: Do we need code changes? We want minimal changes to our runtime.
[00:05:55] Daniel: Most customers make a thin shim — swap base url and param mappings, SDK helper does the rest. If you use streaming you might need a tiny client adapter for event handling, but our SDKs are drop-in for Node/Python.
[00:06:10] Jon: Any gotchas for stop tokens being appended by our infra?
[00:06:13] Daniel: make sure you don't double-escape sequences, but the mapping helper flags those.

[00:06:40] Maya: Ok, let's look at an actual example — here's a chat with system + user + recent history. (reads) We get a bit more verbose on Redwood in the first token window — is that tunable?
[00:06:55] Daniel: yes the sampling params control that; also temperature and presence penalties. For strict parity we recommend setting top_p and temperature to match and run a short A/B.
[00:07:12] Eve: we ran a pilot with another customer where we matched prompt shaping and got p99 within 15ms for most queries after enabling prefix caching.

[00:07:40] Priya: On governance: are audit logs immutable and do they include token deltas?
[00:07:46] Daniel: logs include request/response metadata and byte-level checksums; full content is optionally retained depending on your retention policy and compliance requirements. For PCI/PHI customers we recommend Private with customer-controlled retention and KMS.

[00:08:28] Liam: How does dedicated capacity scale? Can we burst?
[00:08:31] Eve: Dedicated pools have autoscale and burst tiers. You can set baseline commit and enable burst; the routing logic will use burst when needed and we bill accordingly.

[00:09:05] Maya: Pricing model — what's the estimate for our 10M tokens/month?
[00:09:10] Eve: I'll follow up with a tailored estimate, but Optimize can show cost delta after we run a sample pass. We'll include estimated savings for caching and batching.

[00:09:40] Daniel: live parity demo — pasted your OpenAI chat example into the mapping tool. It produced a Redwood payload and we ran it against a similar model variant. Results: responses semantically match JSON sample, minor tokenization differences on edge stop tokens.
[00:10:03] Maya: Can we see the exact diff?
[00:10:05] Daniel: yes here's a side-by-side diff link (shared in chat) — highlights where tokens differ and suggests small prompt adjustments.

[00:11:10] Jon: Is the SDK open source?
[00:11:12] Daniel: yes client libs are open source, we have example adapters for OpenAI-compatible calls.

[00:12:00] Priya: One more security question — SSO + role-based access?
[00:12:04] Eve: SAML SSO supported, and we do RBAC with fine grained roles at project and token levels.

[00:12:30] Maya: ok, what's the expected time-to-pilot? We want to be cautious about the holiday window next month.
[00:12:36] Eve: We can start the equivalence mapping immediately — Daniel can provision a sandbox and run the harness in 1–2 weeks. Full pilot (benchmarks) we usually do over a 1–2 week run once you give the prompt set.

[00:13:02] Daniel: note on KV cache: if your system message is >2k tokens we can reduce repeated compute by caching; you'll need to pin the variant to keep cache stable.
[00:13:18] Liam: Pinning model variants — is that manual?
[00:13:20] Daniel: you can pin via Console or API config; we also have rollout gates for canary A/B.

[00:13:45] Maya: Any limitations migrating from Together's multi-model routing?
[00:13:50] Daniel: we support model ensembles but patterns differ; we usually emulate with routing rules in Redwood and map weights to traffic splits. There's an implementation note in the mapping sheet.

[00:14:30] Eve: quick walkthrough of Optimize suggestions — shows batching recommendations, batch sizes vs latency, and suggested quantization profile. It also shows a per-route cost breakdown so you can see token vs model compute.
[00:14:53] Maya: Those batching suggestions — do they require Colocation or are they runtime-level?
[00:14:58] Daniel: runtime-level. Batching is continuous in the serving runtime; you can tune max wait time and request grouping.

[00:15:30] Priya: For audit requirements we need a 7-year trail, is that supported?
[00:15:35] Daniel: retention is configurable, for Private we can keep long term archives in your S3 bucket. For Hosted we have add-on retention.

[00:16:00] Liam: Ok good. Let's talk about the benchmark run specifics.
[00:16:04] Daniel: we'll want your top 30 prompts, concurrency profile, and production sequence-length distribution. We'll run a 72-hour window with reproducible load to collect p50/p90/p99.
[00:16:18] Maya: We can do that. We'll scrub and anonymize data.

[00:16:50] Eve: last part: proposed timeline and next steps — we'll share the equivalence mapping spreadsheet, security pack, and a draft SOW for a limited pilot. Then schedule bench run.
[00:17:05] Liam: Sounds actionable.

[00:17:30] (wrap-up small talk)
[00:18:00] Eve: recap: Eve to share security docs and pricing estimate; Daniel to provision sandbox and benchmark harness; Maya to share prompt set. We said May 18th for the benchmark window tentative.
[00:18:15] Maya: thanks all.
[00:18:18] (call ends)

Notes about transcription: some proper nouns mis-transcribed (Anthropic->Anthropeek) and some timestamps are approximate.
